I analyzed the jump data from 2023–2026 to find the relationship between jump height and relative propulsive force. I created normative force ranges for different jump heights, visualized those ranges with color-coded charts.

## Normative Relative Force Table

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# 1. Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

jump_data <- read_excel(
  here::here("data", "jump_data.xlsx"),
  sheet = "Sheet6"
)

# 4. Keep the variables needed for this analysis
jump_clean <- jump_data %>%
  select(
    `Jump Height`,
    `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
    `Countermovement Depth`
  ) %>%
  drop_na(
    `Jump Height`,
    `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`
  )


# 5. Create Coach's jump-height ranges
jump_groups <- jump_clean %>%
  mutate(
    jump_range = case_when(
      `Jump Height` >= 25 & `Jump Height` <= 30 ~ "25-30",
      `Jump Height` >= 20 & `Jump Height` < 25 ~ "20-24",
      `Jump Height` >= 15 & `Jump Height` < 20 ~ "15-19",
      `Jump Height` >= 10 & `Jump Height` < 15 ~ "10-14",
      `Jump Height` >= 5  & `Jump Height` < 10 ~ "5-9",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )


# 6. Set the order of the jump-height categories
jump_groups <- jump_groups %>%
  mutate(
    jump_range = factor(
      jump_range,
      levels = c(
        "25-30",
        "20-24",
        "15-19",
        "10-14",
        "5-9"
      )
    )
  )


# 7. Calculate normative statistics for each group
normative_table <- jump_groups %>%
  filter(!is.na(jump_range)) %>%
  group_by(jump_range) %>%
  summarise(
    
    # Number of jumps in the category
    n = n(),
    
    # Average relative propulsive force
    avg_force = mean(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    # Median relative propulsive force
    median_force = median(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    # 25th percentile
    lower_norm = quantile(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      0.25,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    # 75th percentile
    upper_norm = quantile(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      0.75,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    # Standard deviation
    sd_force = sd(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )


# 8. Round the numbers so the table is easy to read
normative_table <- normative_table %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        avg_force,
        median_force,
        lower_norm,
        upper_norm,
        sd_force
      ),
      ~ round(.x, 1)
    )
  )


# 9. Rename columns for the final deliverable
normative_table <- normative_table %>%
  rename(
    `Jump Height Range (in)` = jump_range,
    `Number of Jumps` = n,
    `Average Force (% BW)` = avg_force,
    `Median Force (% BW)` = median_force,
    `Lower Norm - 25th %ile` = lower_norm,
    `Upper Norm - 75th %ile` = upper_norm,
    `Standard Deviation` = sd_force
  )


# 10. View the finished normative table

normative_table %>%
  kable(
    caption = "McCallie Countermovement Jump Normative Data (2023-2026)",
    align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )


```

This table summarizes the jump data by grouping athletes based on how high they jumped. It shows the typical amount of force produced by athletes in each jump-height range and gives us a baseline for what is considered normal at McCallie.

## Color-Coded Normative Force Chart

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

force_chart <- jump_groups %>%
  filter(!is.na(jump_range)) %>%
  group_by(jump_range) %>%
  summarise(
    
    # 25th percentile = bottom of normal range
    lower_norm = quantile(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      0.25,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    # Median = typical force
    median_force = median(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    # 75th percentile = top of normal range
    upper_norm = quantile(
      `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
      0.75,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )


# 2. Make sure jump-height groups appear from lowest to highest

force_chart <- force_chart %>%
  mutate(
    jump_range = factor(
      jump_range,
      levels = c(
        "5-9",
        "10-14",
        "15-19",
        "20-24",
        "25-30"
      )
    )
  )


# 3. Create the color-coded chart

ggplot(force_chart, aes(x = jump_range)) +
  
  # RED: Below expected relative force
  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = as.numeric(jump_range) - 0.4,
      xmax = as.numeric(jump_range) + 0.4,
      ymin = 130,
      ymax = lower_norm
    ),
    fill = "red",
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  
  # GREEN: Normal relative force range
  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = as.numeric(jump_range) - 0.4,
      xmax = as.numeric(jump_range) + 0.4,
      ymin = lower_norm,
      ymax = upper_norm
    ),
    fill = "green",
    alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  
  # BLUE: Above expected relative force
  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = as.numeric(jump_range) - 0.4,
      xmax = as.numeric(jump_range) + 0.4,
      ymin = upper_norm,
      ymax = 300
    ),
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  
  # Median relative force dots
  geom_point(
    aes(y = median_force),
    size = 4
  ) +
  
  # Add median force value above each dot
  geom_text(
    aes(
      y = median_force,
      label = paste0(round(median_force, 1), "%")
    ),
    vjust = -1,
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 4
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "McCallie Relative Propulsive Force Norms",
    subtitle = "Countermovement Jump Data, 2023-2026",
    x = "Jump Height Range (inches)",
    y = "Average Relative Propulsive Force (% Bodyweight)",
    caption = paste(
      "Red = Below Expected |",
      "Green = Normal Range |",
      "Blue = Above Expected"
    )
  ) +
  
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = c(130, 300)
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 12
    ),
    
    axis.title = element_text(
      face = "bold"
    ),
    
    axis.text = element_text(
      size = 11
    )
  )
```

This chart turns the normative data into an easy-to-read visual. The different colors show whether an athlete's force production is below, within, or above the typical range for a certain jump height.

## Force vs. Jump Height Relationship

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

jump_correlation <- cor(
  jump_clean$`Jump Height`,
  jump_clean$`Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

jump_correlation

jump_model <- lm(
  `Jump Height` ~ `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
  data = jump_clean
)
summary(jump_model)

r_squared <- summary(jump_model)$r.squared

r_squared


jump_correlation <- round(jump_correlation, 3)
r_squared <- round(r_squared, 3)

jump_correlation
r_squared


ggplot(
  jump_clean,
  aes(
    x = `Avg. Relative Propulsive Force`,
    y = `Jump Height`
  )
) +
  
  # Each point represents a jump
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.2,
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  
  # Regression line
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Display correlation and R-squared
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = Inf,
    y = -Inf,
    label = paste0(
      "r = ", jump_correlation,
      "\nR² = ", r_squared
    ),
    hjust = 1.2,
    vjust = -1,
    size = 5
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Relative Force and Jump Height",
    subtitle = "McCallie Countermovement Jump Data, 2023-2026",
    x = "Average Relative Propulsive Force (% Bodyweight)",
    y = "Jump Height (inches)",
    caption = "Each point represents a countermovement jump."
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 12
    ),
    
    axis.title = element_text(
      face = "bold"
    ),
    
    axis.text = element_text(
      size = 11
    )
  )


```

This graph shows the overall relationship between how much force an athlete produces relative to their bodyweight and how high they jump. It helps show whether producing more relative force is generally connected to jumping higher.
